nodes.statement: The functions vectqx^2-xk can be expressed as explicit series in H^- (see crefcor:kind2), and can then be meromorphically continued to C; their poles must cancel out in the right-hand side of crefeq:2var-rog-ram since the left-hand side is entire. In fact, dim T_Cleft(qx^2 - xright) = 1 while dim T_H^textnormal-hspace-0.03cmleft(qx^2 - xright) = 2. Also, the Rogers--Ramanujan identities in crefeq:rog-ram follow from the second equality in crefeq:2var-rog-ram by identifying coefficients of x^0 and x^1. In fact, identifying coefficients of x^1-m for m in Z leads to the so-called m-versions of the Rogers--Ramanujan identities, involving sum_n ge 0 q^n^2 + mn/(q; q)_n (see, e.g., ).

First, denote the Dedekind eta function and the generalized Dedekind eta functions of level $N \ge 1$ (following \cite[Corollary 2]{yang2004transformation}) by
\begin{equation} \label{eq:generalized-eta}
    \eta(\tau) := e^{\pi i \tau / 12}(q; q),
    \qquad\qquad 
    \textnormal E_g(\tau) := e^{N B(g/N) \pi i \tau} \left\langle q^g; q^N \right\rangle,
\end{equation}
where $B(t) := t^2 - t + \frac{1}{6}$, $g \in \mathbb{Z}$, and the level $N$ must be specified a priori (the generalized eta functions $\textnormal E_g(\tau)$ should not be confused with the Eisenstein series $E_{2k}(\tau)$).

Then one has the polynomial factorization \[ X^3 - 2fraceta(14tau)^2eta(7tau)^2 X^2 - fraceta(2tau)eta(7tau)^3eta(tau)eta(14tau)^3 X + fraceta(tau)eta(14tau)eta(2tau)eta(7tau) = prod_g = 1^3 left(X - fractextnormal E_g(2tau)textnormal E_3g(tau)right). \]
conclusions: For tau in H^+, let textnormal E_g(tau) denote the generalized eta functions of level N = 7.

Then one has the polynomial factorization \[ X^3 - 2fraceta(14tau)^2eta(7tau)^2 X^2 - fraceta(2tau)eta(7tau)^3eta(tau)eta(14tau)^3 X + fraceta(tau)eta(14tau)eta(2tau)eta(7tau) = prod_g = 1^3 left(X - fractextnormal E_g(2tau)textnormal E_3g(tau)right).
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{cor:eta-poly}
For $\tau \in {\mathbb{H}}^+$, let $\textnormal E_g(\tau)$ denote the generalized eta functions of level $N = 7$. Then one has the polynomial factorization
\[
    X^3
    - 2\frac{\eta(14\tau)^2}{\eta(7\tau)^2} X^2
    - \frac{\eta(2\tau)\eta(7\tau)^3}{\eta(\tau)\eta(14\tau)^3} X
    + \frac{\eta(\tau)\eta(14\tau)}{\eta(2\tau)\eta(7\tau)}

nodes.statement: As noted by Andrews, Schilling and Warnaar , the Rogers--Ramanujan products langle q; q^5 rangle^-1 and langle q^2; q^5 rangle^-1 are characters of a certain textnormal W_2 algebra, which they denote by M(2, 5)_2. We remarked that these products coincide with the q-coefficients of the canonical basis vectors in the septuple identity crefeq:septuple, and explained this correspondence through crefthm:bases-proportional. A similar phenomenon occurs for the octuple (crefprop:octuple) and nonuple (crefprop:nonuple) identities: c|c|c|c|c Algebra & Product identity & Rog.--Ram.\ type id. & 2-Var.\ generaliz. & Correspondence\\ hline M(2, 5)_2 & Septuple, crefeq:septuple & crefeq:rog-ram & crefprop:2var-rog-ram & crefthm:bases-proportional \\ hline M(2, 4)_2 & Octuple, crefeq:octuple & crefeq:rog-ram-var& crefprop:2var-rog-ram-var & crefthm:bases-proportional-2 \\ hline M(3, 7)_3 & Nonuple, crefeq:nonuple & & (Open question) & (Open question) Indeed, the q-coefficients in the right-hand side of the nonuple identity crefeq:nonuple coincide with the 4 characters of the textnormal W_3 algebra M(3, 7)_3 (up to factors of pm 1, pm q, pm 2q), and gives A_2 Rogers--Ramanujan identities for 3 out of these characters (see also ); the more recent work of Corteel and Welsh also provides the fourth identity . Can one complete the bottom row of the table above with an analogue of crefthm:bases-proportional, leading to a new proof of Theorem 1.1 from , and possibly to applications on higher-order mock theta functions? There is also a product identity whose q-coefficients are the characters of M(2, u^2 + v^2)_2, for any relatively prime positive integers u, v such that u + v is odd; see our crefcor:character-identity. These might be connected as in crefqtn:characters to the Andrews--Gordon identities , which generalize crefeq:rog-ram; crefthm:bases-proportional would correspond to the case (u, v) = (1, 1). As pointed out by Professor Ole Warnaar (private communication), the analogue of crefprop:2var-rog-ram in this case could be a summation of variants of the Andrews--Gordon identities as in ; the difficulty lies in relating such a summation to an infinite product in a suitable T_H^textnormal-hspace-0.03cm(f) space.

nodes.statement: Let D subset C be a Z-invariant domain, m a positive integer, and f_1, ldots, f_m meromorphic functions on C/Z (i.e., on C with period 1), with f_m notequiv 0 (i.e., f_m is not the zero function). More generally, given an m times m matrix M(z) whose entries are meromorphic functions on C/Z such that det M(z) notequiv 0, let \[ T_D(M) := left\ vecF in textnormalHol(D/Z)^m : vecF = M cdot T_tau vecF right\, \] where the equality holds as an identity of m meromorphic functions on D cap (D - tau), and (T_tau vecF)(z) = vecF(z+tau) as before. \label{def:T-spaces}
Let $D \subset \mathbb{C}$ be a $\mathbb{Z}$-invariant domain, $m$ a positive integer, and $f_1, \ldots, f_m$ meromorphic functions on $\mathbb{C}/\mathbb{Z}$ (i.e., on $\mathbb{C}$ with period $1$), with $f_m \not\equiv 0$ (i.e., $f_m$ is not the zero function). We define the complex vector space
\[
    \mathcal{T}_D(f_1, \ldots, f_m) := \left\{F \in \textnormal{Hol}(D/\mathbb{Z}) : F = f_1 \cdot T_\tau F + \cdots + f_m \cdot T_{m\tau} F \right\},
\] 
where the equality holds as an identity of meromorphic functions on $D \cap (D - \tau) \cap \cdots \cap (D - m\tau)$. More generally, given an $m \times m$ matrix $M(z)$ whose entries are meromorphic functions on $\mathbb{C}/\mathbb{Z}$ such that $\det M(z) \not\equiv 0$, let
\[
    \mathcal{T}_D(M) := 
    \left\{ 
    \vec{F} \in \textnormal{Hol}(D/\mathbb{Z})^m
    :
    \vec{F} = M \cdot T_\tau \vec{F}
    \right\},
\]
where the equality holds as an identity of $m$ meromorphic functions on $D \cap (D - \tau)$, and $(T_\tau \vec{F})(z) = \vec{F}(z+\tau)$ as before. In particular, we have a linear bijection
\[
    \mathcal{T}_D\left(f_1, \ldots, f_m\right) 
    \ 
    \cong
    \
    \mathcal{T}_{D \cap (D - \tau) \cap \cdots \cap (D - (m-1)\tau)}
    \begin{psmall}
    f_1 & f_2 & \cdots & f_{m-1} & f_m
    \\
    1 & 0 & \cdots & 0 & 0 
    \\
     &  & \ddots &  &   
    \\
    0 & 0 & \cdots & 1 & 0
    \end{psmall}
    \qquad 
    \text{by} \quad
    F \mapsto 
    \begin{psmall}
    F \\
    T_\tau F \\
    \vdots \\
    T_{(m-1)\tau} F
    \end{psmall}.
\]
While much of this paper is concerned with the spaces $\mathcal{T}_D(f)$ (in fact, \cref{sec:higher-prod-id} only works with $\mathcal{T}_D\left(\alpha x^d\right)$), we will encounter more general spaces $\mathcal{T}_D(f_1, \ldots, f_m)$ and $\mathcal{T}_D(M)$ in \cref{sec:rog-ram}.

nodes.name: Two-variable Rogers--Ramanujan fraction
nodes.statement: Consider the entire 1-periodic function F(z) := sum_n ge 0 q^n^2 (q; q)_n^-1 x^n (this is chi(x/q) from ). A short computation shows that \[ forall z in C : F(z) = F(z+tau) + qxF(z+2tau), \] so F = T_tau F + qxT_2tau F and thus F in T_Cleft(1, qxright). This vector space turns out to be one-dimensional, which can be used to prove an identity due to Rogers generalizing the Rogers--Ramanujan identities in crefeq:rog-ram; see crefprop:rogers. By iterating this functional equation in matrix form, one can also recover the Rogers--Ramanujan continued fraction identity , \[ F(z) \\ F(z+tau) = prod_n ge 1 1 & q^n x \\ 1 & 0 cdot 1 \\ 1 Longleftrightarrow fracF(z)F(z+tau) = 1 + fracqx1 + fracq^2x1 + fracq^3 x1 + cdots. \] where the infinite product of matrices above is computed from the left to the right.
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{ex:two-var-rog-ram}
Consider the entire $1$-periodic function $F(z) := \sum_{n \ge 0} q^{n^2} (q; q)_n^{-1} x^n$ (this is $\chi(x/q)$ from \cite[p.~329]{rogers1893second}). A short computation shows that
\[
    \forall z \in \mathbb{C} : \quad F(z) = F(z+\tau) + qxF(z+2\tau),
\]
so $F = T_\tau F + qxT_{2\tau} F$ and thus $F \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(1, qx\right)$. This vector space turns out to be one-dimensional, which can be used to prove an identity due to Rogers generalizing the Rogers--Ramanujan identities in \cref{eq:rog-ram}; see \cref{prop:rogers}. By iterating this functional equation in matrix form, one can also recover the Rogers--Ramanujan continued fraction identity \cite[p.~328 (4)]{rogers1893second},
\[
    \begin{pmatrix}
    F(z)
    \\
    F(z+\tau) 
    \end{pmatrix}
    =
    \prod_{n \ge 1}
    \begin{pmatrix}
    1 & q^n x 
    \\
    1 & 0
    \end{pmatrix}
    \cdot
    \begin{pmatrix}
    1 
    \\
    1
    \end{pmatrix}
    \qquad 
    \Longleftrightarrow 
    \qquad 
    \frac{F(z)}{F(z+\tau)} = 1 + \frac{qx}{1 + \frac{q^2x}{1 + \frac{q^3 x}{1 + \cdots}}}.
\]
where the infinite product of matrices above is computed from the left to the right.

nodes.name: Line bundles and theta functions
nodes.statement: Take D = C and m = 1 in crefdef:T-spaces, and let f be any invertible function in textnormalHol(C/Z). For m, n in Z and z in C, define phi_mtau + n(z) as prod_k=0^m-1 f(z+ktau)^-1 if m ge 0, and as prod_k=-m^-1 f(z+ktau) otherwise. Then (phi_gamma)_gamma in Gamma form a system of multipliers for the lattice Gamma := Ztau + Z, meaning that they are holomorphic invertible and they satisfy the cocycle condition phi_gamma+ delta(z) = phi_gamma(z+delta) phi_delta(z) (see, for example, ). Such a system induces a holomorphic line bundle L cong (C times C)/Gamma over C/Gamma, where gamma in Gamma acts on C times C by gamma(z, t) = (z + gamma, phi_gamma(z)t); a section of this line bundle has the form \[ C/Gamma to L cong left(C times Cright)/Gamma, z mapsto (z, F(z)), \] where F in textnormalHol(C) satisfies F(z + gamma) = phi_gamma(z) F(z), and this reduces to F(z) = f(z)F(z+tau) by our choice of left\phi_gammaright\_gamma in Gamma. Hence the sections of L to C are canonically identified with the elements F of T_C(f), and these are called the theta functions associated to L. Canonical examples are Jacobi's theta functions (see or ), and more generally the functions vectalpha x^dk. While the triple, quintuple, septuple, etc.\ products all lie in such vector spaces induced by invertible functions f, allowing f to have zeros at the cost of reducing the domain of holomorphicity D of F is essential for stating and proving results like crefprop:2var-rog-ram, crefthm:bases-proportional or crefthm:bases-proportional-2. If D contains a horizontal strip of length ge textnormalIm\ tau (thus a copy of C/Gamma), the more general spaces T_D(f) correspond similarly to meromorphic line bundles, while the spaces T_D(M) (where M is an m times m matrix) correspond to vector bundles of rank m (of the form E to C/Gamma where E cong left(C times C^mright)/Gamma) and generalized (or non-abelian) theta functions (see or ). It can be helpful, however, to consider smaller domains D not containing any copy of C/Gamma, as we illustrate crefprop:fractional. For the reader familiar with this language, the properties in the following lemma will come naturally; e.g., creflem:basic.(iii) is motivated by the fact that multiplying a vector bundle by a line bundle yields back a vector bundle of the same rank.
nodes.raw_latex:
Take $D = \mathbb{C}$ and $m = 1$ in \cref{def:T-spaces}, and let $f$ be any invertible function in $\textnormal{Hol}(\mathbb{C}/\mathbb{Z})$. For $m, n \in \mathbb{Z}$ and $z \in \mathbb{C}$, define $\phi_{m\tau + n}(z)$ as $\prod_{k=0}^{m-1} f(z+k\tau)^{-1}$ if $m \ge 0$, and as $\prod_{k=-m}^{-1} f(z+k\tau)$ otherwise. Then $(\phi_\gamma)_{\gamma \in \Gamma}$ form a system of multipliers for the lattice $\Gamma := \mathbb{Z}\tau + \mathbb{Z}$, meaning that they are holomorphic invertible and they satisfy the cocycle condition $\phi_{\gamma+ \delta}(z) = \phi_\gamma(z+\delta) \phi_\delta(z)$ (see, for example, \cite[\S 2.3]{beauville2013theta}). Such a system induces a holomorphic line bundle $L \cong (\mathbb{C} \times \mathbb{C})/\Gamma$ over $\mathbb{C}/\Gamma$, where $\gamma \in \Gamma$ acts on $\mathbb{C} \times \mathbb{C}$ by $\gamma(z, t) = (z + \gamma, \phi_\gamma(z)t)$; a section of this line bundle has the form \[
    \mathbb{C}/\Gamma \to L \cong \left(\mathbb{C} \times \mathbb{C}\right)/\Gamma, 
    \qquad\qquad 
    z \mapsto (z, F(z)),
\]
where $F \in \textnormal{Hol}(\mathbb{C})$ satisfies $F(z + \gamma) = \phi_\gamma(z) F(z)$, and this reduces to $F(z) = f(z)F(z+\tau)$ by our choice of $\left\{\phi_\gamma\right\}_{\gamma \in \Gamma}$. Hence the sections of $L \to C$ are canonically identified with the elements $F$ of $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}(f)$, and these are called the \emph{theta functions} associated to $L$. Canonical examples are Jacobi's theta functions (see \cite{jacobi1829fundamenta} or \cite[p.~464]{whittaker2020course}), and more generally the functions $\vect{\alpha x^d}{k}$.

While the triple, quintuple, septuple, etc.\ products all lie in such vector spaces induced by invertible functions $f$, allowing $f$ to have zeros at the cost of reducing the domain of holomorphicity $D$ of $F$ is essential for stating and proving results like \cref{prop:2var-rog-ram}, \cref{thm:bases-proportional} or \cref{thm:bases-proportional-2}. If $D$ contains a horizontal strip of length $\ge \textnormal{Im}\ \tau$ (thus a copy of $\mathbb{C}/\Gamma$), the more general spaces $\mathcal{T}_D(f)$ correspond similarly to \emph{meromorphic} line bundles, while the spaces $\mathcal{T}_D(M)$ (where $M$ is an $m \times m$ matrix) correspond to \emph{vector} bundles of rank $m$ (of the form $E \to \mathbb{C}/\Gamma$ where $E \cong \left(\mathbb{C} \times \mathbb{C}^m\right)/\Gamma$) and \emph{generalized} (or \emph{non-abelian}) theta functions (see \cite[\S 6.2]{beauville2013theta} or \cite{gunning1982generalized}). It can be helpful, however, to consider smaller domains $D$ not containing any copy of $\mathbb{C}/\Gamma$, as we illustrate \cref{prop:fractional}.



For the reader familiar with this language, the properties in the following lemma will come naturally; e.g., \cref{lem:basic}.(iii) is motivated by the fact that multiplying a vector bundle by a line bundle yields back a vector bundle of the same rank.

\label{lem:basic}
Let $F \in \mathcal{T}_D(f_1, \ldots, f_m)$ and $G \in \mathcal{T}_D(g)$ be as in \cref{def:T-spaces}.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*).]
    \item If $E$ is another $Z$-invariant domain and $\varnothing \neq D \subset E$, then $\mathcal{T}_E(f_1, \ldots, f_m) \subset \mathcal{T}_D(f_1, \ldots, f_m)$,  where a function in $\textnormal{Hol}(E/\mathbb{Z})$ is uniquely identified with its restriction to $\textnormal{Hol}(D/\mathbb{Z})$.
    \item For $w \in \mathbb{C}$, one has $ T_w F \in \mathcal{T}_{D-w}\left(T_w f_1, \ldots, T_w f_m\right)$.
    \item Letting $g_n := \prod_{j=0}^{m-1} T_{j\tau} g$, one has
    $FG \in \mathcal{T}_D\left(f_1 g_1, f_2 g_2, \ldots, f_m g_m\right)$;
    so if $m = 1$, then $FG \in \mathcal{T}_D(f_1g)$. Also, if $G$ has no zeros in $D$, then $G^{-1} \in \mathcal{T}_D(g^{-1})$.
    \item If $u \in \mathbb{Z}$, $u \ge 1$ and $D \cap T_{-\tau} D \cap \cdots \cap T_{-u\tau} D \neq \varnothing$, then
    \[
        S_u G \in \mathcal{T}_{u^{-1}D}\Bigg(\prod_{j=0}^{u-1} S_u T_{j\tau}  g\Bigg).
    \]
    \item If $D$ contains an open horizontal strip of width $> m\cdot \textnormal{Im}\\tau$, then $F$ has a meromorphic continuation to all of $\mathbb{C}$, which still satisfies $F = F_1 \cdot T_\tau F + \cdots + f_m \cdot T_{m\tau} F$.
    \item If $D$ contains an open horizontal strip of width $> \textnormal{Im}\ \tau$, and $0 \neq H \in \mathcal{T}_D(g)$, then $G/H$ extends to an elliptic function on $\mathbb{C}$ with periods $1, \tau$.
\end{enumerate}

Statements (i) and (ii) are immediate, while (iii) and (iv) follow by repeatedly applying (ii) for $w = j\tau$. For (v), let $S \subset D$ be an open horizontal strip of width $> m \cdot \textnormal{Im}\ \tau$; then we can iteratively define $F := f_1 \cdot T_\tau F + \cdots + f_m \cdot T_{m\tau} F$ on the strips $S + n\tau$ for $n \in \{1, 2, 3, \ldots\}$, and
\[
    F := T_{-m\tau} \frac{F - f_1 \cdot T_\tau F - \cdots - f_m T_{m\tau} F}{f_m}
\]
on $S - n\tau$ for $n \in \{1, 2, 3, \ldots\}$; note that $F$ is well-defined on $\mathbb{C}$ by the uniqueness of meromorphic continuation. Finally, (vi) follows from (v) applied to $G$ and $H$, and then (iii) applied for $D' = \mathbb{C} \setminus \{\textnormal{poles of $G$, $H$ or $H^{-1}$}\}$ (one has $H^{-1} \in \mathcal{T}_{D'}(g^{-1})$, and so $G/H \in \mathcal{T}_{D'}(1)$).

nodes.name: Spaces given by constants
nodes.statement: Suppose a domain D contains a horizontal strip S of length > textnormalIm\ tau. Note that T_D(1) = left\ F in textnormalHol(D) : F = T_1 F = T_tau F in D cap (D - tau)right\. The proof of creflem:basic.(ii) then shows that any function F in T_D(1) can be continued to an entire elliptic function on C, thus a constant. More generally, if f_1 equiv alpha is any nonzero constant, then for F in T_D(alpha), considering the Fourier series of F(z) = alpha F(z+tau) in S cap (S - tau) neq varnothing yields \[ widehatF(n) = alpha q^n widehatF(n) \] for any n in Z. So if alpha = q^-n for some n in Z, we find that T_D(alpha) is one-dimensional, spanned by x^n; otherwise, T_D(alpha) = \0\. We give a more general upper bound for dim T_D in crefprop:upper-bounds.
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{ex:constants}
Suppose a domain $D$ contains a horizontal strip $S$ of length $> \textnormal{Im}\ \tau$. Note that $\mathcal{T}_D(1) = \left\{ F \in \textnormal{Hol}(D) : F = T_1 F = T_\tau F \text{ in } D \cap (D - \tau)\right\}$.

The proof of \cref{lem:basic}.(ii) then shows that any function $F \in \mathcal{T}_D(1)$ can be continued to an \emph{entire} elliptic function on $\mathbb{C}$, thus a constant. More generally, if $f_1 \equiv \alpha$ is any nonzero constant, then for $F \in \mathcal{T}_D(\alpha)$, considering the Fourier series of $F(z) = \alpha F(z+\tau)$ in $S \cap (S - \tau) \neq \varnothing$ yields 
\[
    \widehat{F}(n) = \alpha q^n \widehat{F}(n)
\] 
for any $n \in \mathbb{Z}$. So if $\alpha = q^{-n}$ for some $n \in \mathbb{Z}$, we find that $\mathcal{T}_D(\alpha)$ is one-dimensional, spanned by $x^n$; otherwise, $\mathcal{T}_D(\alpha) = \{0\}$. We give a more general upper bound for $\dim \mathcal{T}_D$ in \cref{prop:upper-bounds}.

\label{prop:upper-bounds}
Let $P_0(z), P_1(z), \ldots, P_m(z)$ be complex polynomials in $x = e^{2\pi i z}$ with $P_0 \neq 0$ and $\big(\widehat{P_0}(0), \ldots, \widehat{P_m}(0)\big) \neq (0, \ldots, 0)$, and let $d := \max(\deg_x P_0, \ldots, \deg_x P_m)$. For $1 \le j \le m$, take $f_j := P_j/P_0$. Suppose $D \subset \mathbb{C}$ is a $\mathbb{Z}$-invariant domain, containing an open horizontal strip $S$ of width $> m \cdot \textnormal{Im}\ \tau$. Letting $V := \mathcal{T}_D\left(f_1, \ldots, f_m\right)$, the following hold true.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*).]
    \item
One has $\dim V \le d + m$. 
    \item
For $n \in \mathbb{Z}$, denote $A_n := P_0 - q^n P_1 - \cdots - q^{mn} P_m$. Assume additionally that $\exists n_0 \in \mathbb{Z}$,
\[
\forall n \ge n_0 + d :\  \widehat{A_n}(0) \neq 0  \qquad \text{ and } \qquad \forall n < n_0 :\  \widehat{A_n}(d) \neq 0.
\]
Then one has $\dim V \le d$, with equality iff $\forall k \in \{0, 1, \ldots, d-1\}$, $\exists F_k \in V$ such that
\[
    \widehat{F_k}(j) = \mathbbm{1}_{j = n_0 + k} \quad \text{ in } S, \quad\quad\hspace{0.2cm}  \forall j \in \{0, 1, \ldots, d-1\},
\]
In this case, $\{F_0, \ldots, F_{d-1}\}$ is a (uniquely determined) basis of $V$.
\end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Proof of \cref{prop:upper-bounds}
nodes.statement: For F in T_D(f_1, ldots, f_m), we have F = f_1 cdot T_tau F + cdots + f_m cdot T_mtau F and thus P_0 cdot F = P_1 cdot T_tau F + cdots + P_m cdot T_mtau F. Taking the Fourier series in S cap (S - mtau) neq varnothing then yields \[ forall n in Z : sum_k=0^d widehatP_0(k) widehatF(n-k) = sum_j=1^m sum_k=0^d widehatP_j(k) q^j(n-k) widehatF(n-k), \] which rearranges (by subtracting the right side from the left side and swapping sums) to sum_k=0^d widehatA_n-k(k) widehatF(n-k) = 0. If d = 0, we find that widehatF(n) = 0 whenever widehatA_n(0) neq 0. So (ii) holds trivially since if all widehatA_n(0) neq 0, we must have F = 0. For statement (i), note that one can have widehatA_n(0) = 0 for at most m values of n, say among \n_1, ldots, n_m\, since widehatA_n(0) is a nonzero polynomial in q^n of degree le m. Hence V injects linearly into a subspace of C^m by the map F mapsto big(widehatF(n_1), ldots, widehatF(n_m) big), proving dim V le m. Now assume that d ge 1. When widehatA_n(0) neq 0, crefeq:recursion implies that widehatF(n) is a linear function of widehatF(n-1), ldots, widehatF(n-d). Similarly, when widehatA_n(d) neq 0, widehatF(n) is a linear function of widehatF(n+1), ldots, widehatF(n+d). Hence under the assumption of (ii), V injects linearly into C^d by F mapsto big(widehatF(n_0), ldots, widehatF(n_0 + d-1)big), proving that dim V = d with equality iff each standard basis vector of C^d is attained by this injection; the preimages of these vectors correspond to F_0, ldots, F_d-1. For $F \in \mathcal{T}_D(f_1, \ldots, f_m)$, we have $F = f_1 \cdot T_\tau F + \cdots + f_m \cdot T_{m\tau} F$ and thus $P_0 \cdot F = P_1 \cdot T_\tau F + \cdots + P_m \cdot T_{m\tau} F$. Taking the Fourier series in $S \cap (S - m\tau) \neq \varnothing$ then yields 
\[
    \forall n \in \mathbb{Z} : \qquad\quad \sum_{k=0}^d \widehat{P_0}(k) \widehat{F}(n-k)
    =
    \sum_{j=1}^m \sum_{k=0}^d \widehat{P_j}(k) q^{j(n-k)} \widehat{F}(n-k),
\]
which rearranges (by subtracting the right side from the left side and swapping sums) to
\begin{equation}\label{eq:recursion}
    \sum_{k=0}^d \widehat{A_{n-k}}(k) \widehat{F}(n-k) = 0.
\end{equation}
If $d = 0$, we find that $\widehat{F}(n) = 0$ whenever $\widehat{A_n}(0) \neq 0$. So (ii) holds trivially since if all $\widehat{A_n}(0) \neq 0$, we must have $F = 0$. Now assume that $d \ge 1$. When $\widehat{A_n}(0) \neq 0$, \cref{eq:recursion} implies that $\widehat{F}(n)$ is a linear function of $\widehat{F}(n-1), \ldots, \widehat{F}(n-d)$. \label{lem:basic-S}
Let $D$ be a $\mathbb{Z}$-invariant domain and $f, g$ be meromorphic functions on $\mathbb{C}/\mathbb{Z}$.
\begin{enumerate}[label = (\roman*).]
    \item If $F \in \mathcal{S}_D(f)$ and $G \in \mathcal{S}_D(g)$, then $FG \in \mathcal{S}_D(fg)$. 
    \item If $D \cap (-D) \neq \varnothing$ and $\mathcal{S}_D(g) \neq \{0\}$, then one has $g(z)g(-z) = 1$ wherever defined.
    \item If $D \cap (-D) \cap (D-\tau) \cap (-D-\tau) \neq \varnothing$ and $\mathcal{T}_D(f) \cap \mathcal{S}_D(g) \neq \{0\}$, then wherever defined,
    \[
        f(z)f(-z-\tau) = g(z)g(-z-\tau).
    \]
    
    
    
    
\end{enumerate}

Then as in crefeq:recursion we have widehatF(n) = alpha q^n-d widehatF(n-d) for all n in Z. Fixing a nonzero Fourier coefficient widehatF(n_0), we find inductively that widehatF(n_0 - nd) grows on the order of q^dn^2/2, which contradicts the convergence of the Fourier series of F anywhere since leftvert q^drightvert > 1. Now suppose that d > 0. Take m = 1, P_0(z) = 1 and P_1(z) = alpha x^d in crefprop:upper-bounds, and consider A_n(z) = 1 - alpha q^n x^d. We have widehatA_n(0) neq 0 and widehatA_n(d) neq 0 for all n in Z, so crefprop:upper-bounds.(ii) yields that dim T_Dleft(alpha x^d right) le d, with equality iff there exist \F_k\_0 le k < d subset T_Dleft(alpha x^d right) such that widehatF_k(j) = mathbbm1_j=k, forall j, k in \0, 1, ldots, d-1\, where the Fourier series are taken in S. Such functions are the canonical basis vectors from crefsec:intro, \[ left\vectalpha x^dkright\_0 le k < d = left\sum_n in Z alpha^n q^dbinomn2+k_jnx^dn+kright\_0 le k < d, \] given by locally uniformly convergent Fourier series in z in C supset D. Write $f(z) = \alpha x^d \cdot g(-z)$, where $\alpha = \widehat{f}(d)$ and $g(z)$ is a polynomial in $x$ with free coefficient $\widehat{g}(0) = 1$. Then consider the function
\[
    G(z) := \prod_{n \ge 1} g(-z + n\tau) = \prod_{n \ge 1} \left(1 + \widehat{g}(1) q^nx^{-1} + \widehat{g}(2) q^{2n}x^{-2} + \cdots \right),
\]
where the product converges locally uniformly in $\mathbb{C}$ (given that $\sum_{n \ge 1} q^n$ converges); note that $G$ is designed to satisfy $G(z)g(-z) = G(z+\tau)$, hence $G \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(g(-z)^{-1}\right)$. Moreover, since $f(z)$ is nonzero on $\{\textnormal{Im}\ z < - \textnormal{Im}\ \tau\}$, each $g(-z+n\tau)$ is nonzero on $\{\textnormal{Im}\ z < (n-1)\textnormal{Im}\ \tau\}$, so $G$ is nonzero on $\{\textnormal{Im}\ z < 0\} = {\mathbb{H}}^-$ by standard properties of infinite products, and thus $G^{-1} \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{-}\hspace{-0.03cm}}}\left(g(-z)\right)$. Applying \cref{lem:basic}.(iii) twice, we find that multiplication by $G(z)$ induces a bijective linear map
\begin{equation}\label{eq:bijection}
     \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{-}\hspace{-0.03cm}}} (f)
     \xlongrightarrow{\cdot\ G(z)}
     \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{-}\hspace{-0.03cm}}}\big(\alpha x^d \big)
     =
     \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\big(\alpha x^d \big),
\end{equation}
proving $\dim \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{-}\hspace{-0.03cm}}}(f) = \dim \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(\alpha x^d\right) = d$ by \cref{prop:monomial-spaces}. By \cref{lem:basic}.(i), this immediately implies that $\dim \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}(f) \le d$. Now say $f(z)$ is not a monomial in $x$, so it must have a zero $z_0 \in \mathbb{C}$, which results in a zero $w_0$ of $G(z)$. For $k \in \mathbb{Z}$, consider the product
\[
    F_k(z) := x^k \big\langle {-\alpha} q^k x^d; q^d \big\rangle \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\big(q^{-k} \cdot \alpha q^k x^d\big) = \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\big(\alpha x^d\big).
\]
Then $F_0(z)$ has zeros precisely when $-\alpha x^d = q^{nd}$ for some $n \in \mathbb{Z}$, i.e.\ when $z = u + (dn\tau + 2m\pi i)/d$ for some $m \in \mathbb{Z}$ and a fixed $u \in \mathbb{C}$. Hence $F_k(z) = x^k F_0(z + k\tau/d) = 0$ iff $z = u + ((dn-k)+ 2m\pi i)/d$ for some $m \in \mathbb{Z}$, which implies that $F_j$ and $F_k$ have no common zeros when $j \not\equiv k \pmod{d}$. So assuming $d \ge 2$, there is some $F_j$ with $F_j(w_0) \neq 0$, which implies that
\[
    F_j \cdot G^{-1} \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{-}\hspace{-0.03cm}}}(f) \setminus \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}(f)
    \qquad 
    \Rightarrow 
    \qquad 
    \dim \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}(f) < d.
\]
This settles the equality case of $\dim \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}(f) \le d$ (together with \cref{prop:monomial-spaces}.(i)). The statement about zeros in fundamental regions of ${\mathbb{H}}^-$ follows from the analogous statement in \cref{prop:monomial-spaces}.(i) and the bijection in \cref{eq:bijection} (since $G$ has no zeros in ${\mathbb{H}}^-$).

\label{prop:canonical-basis-vectors}
Let $f(z)$ be a polynomial in $x = e^{2\pi i z}$ with $\deg_x f = d \ge 1$, such that $f(z)$ has no zeros in $\{\textnormal{Im}\ z < -\textnormal{Im}\ \tau\}$, and $\widehat{f}(0) \not\in \left\{q^{-n} : n \ge d \right\}$. \]

For $f(z) = qx^2 - x$ and $k \in \{0, 1\}$, $\vect{qx^2-x}{k}$ is a well-defined holomorphic function in ${\mathbb{H}}^-$ by \cref{prop:polynomial-spaces}. By \cref{lem:basic}.(v), it can be continued meromorphically to $\mathbb{C}$, with simple poles at $z = n\tau + m$ for $n, m \in \mathbb{Z}$ with $n \ge 0$; these poles are cancelled when multiplying by $\left(x^{-1}; q\right)$, as expected since we know $\left(x^{-1}; q\right)\vect{qx^2 - x}{k} \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(qx^2\right)$ is entire. Using \cref{eq:triple}, \cref{eq:quintuple}, and our main result in \cref{thm:bases-proportional}, one can easily compute the residues of these functions at the periodic poles $z \in \mathbb{Z}$; up to a factor of $2\pi i$, these are
\[
    \lim_{x \to 1} (x-1)\vect{qx^2 - x}{k}
    =
    \begin{cases}
    \left\langle q; q^5 \right\rangle^{-1}, &k = 0, \\
    \left\langle q^2; q^5 \right\rangle^{-1}, &k = 1,
    \end{cases}
\]
which is consistent with the pole cancellation in \cref{prop:2var-rog-ram}. One can also verify this numerically as an identity of $q$-series: expand $F(z) := \vect{qx^2-x}{k} = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \widehat{F}(n) x^n$ in ${\mathbb{H}}^-$ and write
\[
    \lim_{x \to 1} (x-1)\vect{qx^2 - x}{k} =
    \lim_{n \to -\infty} \widehat{F}(n),
\]
since $(x-1)\vect{qx^2 - x}{k}$ has the Fourier series $\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \big(\widehat{F}(n-1) - \widehat{F}(n)\big) x^n$ in $\left\{\textnormal{Im}\ z < \textnormal{Im}\ \tau \right\} \supset \mathbb{Z}$, and $\widehat{F}(n) \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$ (note that $\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \widehat{F}(n) x^n$ converges absolutely for $z \in {\mathbb{H}}^-$, i.e.\ $|x| > 1$).

nodes.statement: Note that left(beta q^d+k; q^dright)_n has no zeros for n ge 0 by our assumption on beta, and in fact we have left(beta q^d+k; q^dright)_n^-1 = 1 + O(q) = O(1) for n ge 0; hence the coefficients of x^dn+k in the middle series above decrease like q^dn^2/2. For n < 0, we defined left(beta q^d+k; q^dright)_n = left(beta q^d+k-dn; q^dright)_-n^-1, and thus \[ fracalpha^n q^dbinomn2+knbig(beta q^d+k; q^d big)_n = alpha^n q^dbinomn2+kn prod_j=1^|n| left(1 - beta q^d+k-djright) &= alpha^-|n| q^dbinom|n|+12-k|n| cdot Oleft(|beta|^|n| |q|^sum_j=1^|n| (d+k-dj) right) \\ &= Oleft(|q^dbeta/alpha|^|n| right). \] assuming without loss of generality that beta neq 0 (when the given series coincides with vectalpha x^dk). But since alpha x^d + beta neq 0 in the range \textnormalIm\ z < -textnormalIm\ tau\ (when |x^d| spans left(|q|^-d, +inftyright)), we must have |beta/alpha| le |q|^-d, i.e.\ |q^d beta / alpha| le 1. Hence the bound above reduces to O(1). This shows that the middle series in crefeq:kind1 converges absolutely and locally uniformly to a holomorphic function R(z) for z in H^- (using that |x^-1| < 1 to bound sum_n < 0 x^dn+k, and the quadratic-exponent decrease of q^dn(n-1)/2 x^n for n ge 0). We clearly have widehatR(j) = mathbbm1_j=k for 0 le j < d, so to prove the first equality in crefeq:kind1 it remains to show that R in T_H^textnormal-hspace-0.03cm(alpha x^d + beta). Indeed, we have \[ left(alpha x^d + betaright) R(z+tau) &= sum_n in Z alpha^n+1 fracq^dbinomn+12+k(n+1)left(beta q^d+k; q^dright)_n x^d(n+1)+k + beta sum_n in Z alpha^n fracq^dbinomn+12+k(n+1)left(beta q^d+k; q^dright)_n x^dn+k \\ &= sum_n in Z alpha^n fracq^dbinomn2+knleft(beta q^d+k; q^dright)_n x^dn+k left(1 - beta q^d+k+d(n-1) + beta q^dn+k right) = R(z). \] For the second equality in crefeq:kind1, we require two simple identities that will be proven (non-circularly) in the next subsection: crefeq:basic1 and crefeq:basic2. For z in H^-, consider the function \[ F(z) := fracvectalpha x^dkleft(-alpha^-1beta x^-d q^d; q^dright) \ stackrelby crefeq:basic2=joinrel=joinrel= \ sum_n in Z alpha^n q^dbinomn2 + kn x^dn+k cdot sum_n ge 0 frac1left(q^d; q^dright)_n big(-alpha^-1beta x^-d q^d big)^n. \] We have F in T_H^textnormal-hspace-0.03cmleft(alpha x^dleft(1 + alpha^-1beta x^-dright) right) = T_H^textnormal-hspace-0.03cmleft(alpha x^d + beta right) by creftbl:spaces, and thus F has a basis representation as in crefeq:fourier-coeffs-basis. But by multiplying out the Fourier series above, we see that \[ forall j in \0, 1, ldots, d-1\ : widehatF(j) = 0, &j neq k, \\ sum_n ge 0 fracq^dbinomn2left(q^d; q^dright)_n left(-beta q^d+kright)^n, &j = k, \] and the latter sum reduces to left(beta q^d+k; q^d right) by crefeq:basic1. nodes.raw_latex:
Note that $\left(\beta q^{d+k}; q^d\right)_n$ has no zeros for $n \ge 0$ by our assumption on $\beta$, and in fact we have $\left(\beta q^{d+k}; q^d\right)_n^{-1} = 1 + O(q) = O(1)$ for $n \ge 0$; hence the coefficients of $x^{dn+k}$ in the middle series above decrease like $q^{dn^2/2}$. For $n < 0$, we defined $\left(\beta q^{d+k}; q^d\right)_n = \left(\beta q^{d+k-dn}; q^d\right)_{-n}^{-1}$, and thus 
\[
\begin{aligned}
    \frac{\alpha^n q^{d\binom{n}{2}+kn}}{\big(\beta q^{d+k}; q^d \big)_n} =
    \alpha^n q^{d\binom{n}{2}+kn}
    \prod_{j=1}^{|n|} \left(1 - \beta q^{d+k-dj}\right)
    &=
    \alpha^{-|n|} q^{d\binom{|n|+1}{2}-k|n|} \cdot
    O\left(|\beta|^{|n|} |q|^{\sum_{j=1}^{|n|} (d+k-dj)} \right)
    \\
    &=
    O\left(|q^d\beta/\alpha|^{|n|} \right).
\end{aligned}
\]
assuming without loss of generality that $\beta \neq 0$ (when the given series coincides with $\vect{\alpha x^d}{k}$). But since $\alpha x^d + \beta \neq 0$ in the range $\{\textnormal{Im}\ z < -\textnormal{Im}\ \tau\}$ (when $|x^d|$ spans $\left(|q|^{-d}, +\infty\right)$), we must have $|\beta/\alpha| \le |q|^{-d}$, i.e.\ $|q^d \beta / \alpha| \le 1$. Hence the bound above reduces to $O(1)$.

This shows that the middle series in \cref{eq:kind1} converges absolutely and locally uniformly to a holomorphic function $R(z)$ for $z \in {\mathbb{H}}^-$ (using that $|x^{-1}| < 1$ to bound $\sum_{n < 0} x^{dn+k}$, and the quadratic-exponent decrease of $q^{dn(n-1)/2} x^n$ for $n \ge 0$). We clearly have $\widehat{R}(j) = \mathbbm{1}_{j=k}$ for $0 \le j < d$, so to prove the first equality in \cref{eq:kind1} it remains to show that $R \in \mathcal{T}_{{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{-}\hspace{-0.03cm}}}}(\alpha x^d + \beta)$. Indeed, we have
\[
\begin{aligned}
    \left(\alpha x^d + \beta\right) R(z+\tau)
    &=
    \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}}
    \alpha^{n+1}
    \frac{q^{d\binom{n+1}{2}+k(n+1)}}{\left(\beta q^{d+k}; q^d\right)_n} x^{d(n+1)+k}
    +
    \beta \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \alpha^n \frac{q^{d\binom{n+1}{2}+k(n+1)}}{\left(\beta q^{d+k}; q^d\right)_n} x^{dn+k}
    \\
    &=
    \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \alpha^n \frac{q^{d\binom{n}{2}+kn}}{\left(\beta q^{d+k}; q^d\right)_n} x^{dn+k} \left(1 - \beta q^{d+k+d(n-1)} + \beta q^{dn+k} \right)
    \quad =
    R(z).
\end{aligned}
\]
For the second equality in \cref{eq:kind1}, we require two simple identities that will be proven (non-circularly) in the next subsection: \cref{eq:basic1} and \cref{eq:basic2}. For $z \in {\mathbb{H}}^-$, consider the function
\[
    F(z) := \frac{\vect{\alpha x^d}{k}}{\left(-\alpha^{-1}\beta x^{-d} q^d; q^d\right)}
    \
    \stackrel{\text{by \cref{eq:basic2}}}{=\joinrel=\joinrel=}
    \
    \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \alpha^n q^{d\binom{n}{2} + kn} x^{dn+k} \cdot \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{1}{\left(q^d; q^d\right)_n} \big({-\alpha^{-1}\beta} x^{-d} q^d \big)^n.
\]
We have $F \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{-}\hspace{-0.03cm}}}\left(\alpha x^d\left(1 + \alpha^{-1}\beta x^{-d}\right) \right) = \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{-}\hspace{-0.03cm}}}\left(\alpha x^d + \beta \right)$ by \cref{tbl:spaces}, and thus $F$ has a basis representation as in \cref{eq:fourier-coeffs-basis}. But by multiplying out the Fourier series above, we see that
\[
    \forall j \in \{0, 1, \ldots, d-1\} : \qquad\quad 
    \widehat{F}(j) = 
    \begin{cases}
        0, &j \neq k, \\
        \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{d\binom{n}{2}}}{\left(q^d; q^d\right)_n} \left(-\beta q^{d+k}\right)^n,
        &j = k,
    \end{cases}
\]
and the latter sum reduces to $\left(\beta q^{d+k}; q^d \right)$ by \cref{eq:basic1}. We thus have $F(z) = \left(\beta q^{d+k}; q^d \right) \vect{\alpha x^d + \beta}{k}$, completing our proof.

First, recall from the proof of \cref{prop:polynomial-spaces} that $G \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(g(-z)^{-1}\right)$ is well-defined and multiplication by $G$ induces a bijection $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{-}\hspace{-0.03cm}}}(f) \to \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{-}\hspace{-0.03cm}}}(\alpha x^d)$ as in $\cref{eq:bijection}$.
We leave to the reader to verify that the series in the right-hand side of \cref{eq:kind2} converges absolutely and locally uniformly for $z \in {\mathbb{H}}^-$ to a function $R(z)$, which is similar to the proof of \cref{prop:exact-formulae-kind1}; the fact that $\widehat{f}(0) = 0$ and thus $\deg_x g \le d-1$ is crucial here, to ensure that $\widehat{R}(n)$ decreases like $q^{cn^2}$ as $n \to \infty$ for some $c > 0$. Now $R(z)G(z)$ is just a \emph{twisted} version of the series $\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \alpha^n q^{d\binom{n}{2}+kn} x^{dn+k}$ in the sense of \cref{eq:w-coeffs}; thus $R \cdot G \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{-}\hspace{-0.03cm}}}\left(\alpha x^d\right)$, and so $R \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{-}\hspace{-0.03cm}}} (f)$. 

It remains to identify the Fourier coefficients $\widehat{R}(j)$ for $0 \le j < d$. Note that the Fourier expansions of $G(z + (n-1)\tau)/G(z)$ and $g_k(-z-(n-1)\tau)$ only contain negative powers of $x$, so only the terms $n \ge 0$ in $\cref{eq:kind2}$ contribute to the Fourier coefficients $\{\widehat{R}(j)\}_{0 \le j < d}$. But for $n \ge 1$, one has
\[
    x^{dn+k}
    \frac{G\left(z+(n-1)\tau\right)}{G(z)} g_k\left(-z-(n-1)\tau\right)
    =
    x^{dn+k}
    \Bigg(\prod_{j=2-n}^0 g(-z+j\tau)\Bigg)
    \Bigg( \sum_{j=0}^k \widehat{g}(j) \left(q^{n-1} x\right)^{-j}\Bigg),
\]
which only contains powers of $x$ with exponents $\ge dn+k - (d-1)(n-1) - k \ge d$. Hence the only relevant term is the one given by $n = 0$, which is
\[
    x^k \frac{G(z-\tau)}{G(z)} g_k(-z+\tau)
    =
    x^k \frac{g_k(-z+\tau)}{g(-z+\tau)}
    =
    x^k - x^k\frac{g(-z+\tau) - g_k(-z+\tau)}{g(-z+\tau)}.
\] 
But by the definition of $g_k$, the difference $g(-z+\tau) - g_k(-z+\tau)$ only contains powers of $x$ with exponents less than $-k$. We conclude that $\widehat{R}(j) = \mathbbm{1}_{j=k}$ for $0 \le j < d$, and thus $R = \vect{f}{k}$.

\label{lem:proofs-by-fourier}
Suppose $\mathcal{T}_D(f_1, \ldots, f_m)$, $S \subset D$, $d \ge 1$ and $n_0 \in \mathbb{Z}$ are as in the hypothesis of \cref{prop:upper-bounds}.(ii). Then given $F, G \in \mathcal{T}_D(f_1, \ldots, f_m)$, one has $F = G$ iff $\widehat{F}(k) = \widehat{G}(k)$ for all $k \in \{n_0, n_0 + 1, \ldots, n_0 + d-1\}$ (taking Fourier series in the strip $S$). If $d = 1$ and the limits below exist and are nonzero, one also has
\[
    F = G \qquad 
    \iff 
    \qquad \lim_{n \to \infty} \widehat{F}(n) 
    =
    \lim_{n \to \infty} \widehat{G}(n).
\]

nodes.statement: It suffices to prove the claim when |b/a| < |q| and a not in \q^n : n in Z\, by the uniqueness of analytic continuation in a. Letting D := \z : |b/a| < |x| < 1\, we note that D includes a horizontal strip of length > textnormalIm\ tau, and that both sides of crefeq:ramanujan-1psi1 yield holomorphic functions of z inside D. Using creftbl:spaces, the right-hand side lies in \[ T_Dleft(frac-ax(1-x)(1-b/aqx)^-1 right) = T_Dleft(frac(b/q) - ax1-xright), \] and the same is easily verified for the left-hand side. In the context of crefprop:upper-bounds.(ii), we have A_n(z) = 1 - x - q^n((b/q) + ax); hence d = 1, widehatA_n(0) = 1 - q^n-1b neq 0 for any n ge 1, and widehatA_n(d) = q^n a - 1 neq 0 for any n < 0. Thus the conditions in crefprop:upper-bounds.(ii) are fulfilled for n_0 = 0, and so by creflem:proofs-by-fourier it suffices to check that lim_n to infty widehatF(n) = lim_n to infty widehatG(n), where F and G denote the left-hand side and the right-hand side of crefeq:ramanujan-1psi1. But clearly \[ lim_n to infty widehatF(n) = frac(a; q)(b; q) neq 0. \] Concerning the right-hand side, note that (1-x)G(z) extends to a holomorphic function on D' := \z : |b/a| < |x| < |q|^-1\; hence the Fourier series (1-x)G(z) = sum_n in Z left(widehatG(n) - widehatG(n-1)right) x^n extends to (and converges absolutely and locally uniformly in) D'. Plugging in x = 1 yields \[ lim_x to 1 (1-x)G(z) = sum_n in Z left(widehatG(n) - widehatG(n-1)right), \] where the sum converges absolutely. But the fact that sum_n in Z widehatG(n) x^n also converges absolutely for some |x| < 1 forces lim_n to -infty widehatG(n) = 0, and thus \[ lim_n to infty widehatG(n) = lim_x to 1 (1-x)G(z) = frac(q; q)(b/a; q)(b; q)(q/a; q) frac(a; q)(q/a; q)(q; q)(b/a; q) = frac(a; q)(b; q), \] which completes our proof.

It suffices to prove the claim when $|b/a| < |q|$ and $a \not \in \{q^n : n \in \mathbb{Z}\}$, by the uniqueness of analytic continuation in $a$. Letting $D := \{z : |b/a| < |x| < 1\}$, we note that $D$ includes a horizontal strip of length $> \textnormal{Im}\ \tau$, and that both sides of \cref{eq:ramanujan-1psi1} yield holomorphic functions of $z$ inside $D$. Using \cref{tbl:spaces}, the right-hand side lies in
\[
    \mathcal{T}_D\left(\frac{-ax}{(1-x)(1-b/aqx)^{-1}} \right)
    =
    \mathcal{T}_D\left(\frac{(b/q) - ax}{1-x}\right),
\]
and the same is easily verified for the left-hand side. In the context of \cref{prop:upper-bounds}.(ii), we have $A_n(z) = 1 - x - q^n((b/q) + ax)$; hence $d = 1$, $\widehat{A_n}(0) = 1 - q^{n-1}b \neq 0$ for any $n \ge 1$, and $\widehat{A_n}(d) = q^n a - 1 \neq 0$ for any $n < 0$. Thus the conditions in \cref{prop:upper-bounds}.(ii) are fulfilled for $n_0 = 0$, and so by \cref{lem:proofs-by-fourier} it suffices to check that $\lim_{n \to \infty} \widehat{F}(n) = \lim_{n \to \infty} \widehat{G}(n)$, where $F$ and $G$ denote the left-hand side and the right-hand side of \cref{eq:ramanujan-1psi1}. But clearly
\[
    \lim_{n \to \infty} \widehat{F}(n) = \frac{(a; q)}{(b; q)} \neq 0.
\]
Concerning the right-hand side, note that $(1-x)G(z)$ extends to a holomorphic function on $D' := \{z : |b/a| < |x| < |q|^{-1}\}$; hence the Fourier series $(1-x)G(z) = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \left(\widehat{G}(n) - \widehat{G}(n-1)\right) x^n$ extends to (and converges absolutely and locally uniformly in) $D'$. Plugging in $x = 1$ yields
\[
    \lim_{x \to 1} (1-x)G(z) 
    =
    \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \left(\widehat{G}(n) - \widehat{G}(n-1)\right),
\]
where the sum converges absolutely. But the fact that $\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \widehat{G}(n) x^n$ also converges absolutely for some $|x| < 1$ forces $\lim_{n \to -\infty} \widehat{G}(n) = 0$, and thus
\[
    \lim_{n \to \infty} \widehat{G}(n) = \lim_{x \to 1} (1-x)G(z)
    =
    \frac{(q; q)(b/a; q)}{(b; q)(q/a; q)} \frac{(a; q)(q/a; q)}{(q; q)(b/a; q)}
    =
    \frac{(a; q)}{(b; q)},
\]
which completes our proof.

nodes.statement: For z in C and any N ge 1, \[ (x; q)_N left(q/x; qright)_N = sum_n = -N^N frac(q; q)_2N(q; q)_N-n (q; q)_N+n (-1)^n q^binomn2 x^n. \] Taking N to infty recovers Jacobi's triple product identity from crefeq:triple.

\label{prop:Cauchy} 
For $z \in \mathbb{C}$ and any $N \ge 1$,

\]
Taking $N \to \infty$ recovers Jacobi's triple product identity from \cref{eq:triple}.

To show that $(q; q) \left\langle x; q\right\rangle \left\langle qx^2; q^2\right\rangle = \vect{qx^3}{0} - \vect{qx^3}{1}$, it is easier to take $x \mapsto -x$ and prove 
\[
    (q; q) \left\langle -x; q\right\rangle \left\langle qx^2; q^2\right\rangle \stackrel{?}{=} \left(q^3; q^3\right)\left(\left\langle qx^3; q^3 \right\rangle + x\left\langle q^2 x^3; q^3 \right\rangle \right)
\]
instead (where we used \cref{eq:canonical-formula} on the right-hand side). Both sides lie in $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(-qx^3\right) \cap \mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(x\right)$ by multiplying the respective factors in \cref{tbl:spaces}, which is one-dimensional by \cref{prop:monomial-spaces}, and spanned by $\vect{-qx^3}{0} + \vect{-qx^3}{1}$. Hence both sides have $\widehat{F}(2) = 0$, and by \cref{lem:proofs-by-value} it suffices to check the equality when $x = \zeta$ is a cube root of unity. The latter reduces to
\[
    (q; q) \left( -\zeta; q\right) \left( -q\zeta^2; q\right) 
    \left( q\zeta^2; q^2\right) \left( q\zeta; q^2\right) 
    \stackrel{?}{=} \left(q^3; q^3\right)\left(\left\langle q; q^3 \right\rangle + \zeta \left\langle q^2; q^3 \right\rangle \right).
\]
Using $(-\zeta; q) = (1 + \zeta)(-q\zeta; q)$ and simplifying by $(q; q)(1+\zeta)$, this further reduces to
\[
    \left( -q\zeta; q\right) \left( -q\zeta^2; q\right) 
    \left( q\zeta; q^2\right)\left( q\zeta^2; q^2\right)
    \stackrel{?}{=} 1.
\]
Finally, using $(-x; q) = \left(x^2; q^2\right)/(x; q)$, the left-hand side becomes \[
    \frac{\left( q^2\zeta^2; q^2\right) \left( q^2\zeta; q^2\right) 
    \left( q\zeta; q^2\right)\left( q\zeta^2; q^2\right)}
    {\left( q\zeta; q\right) \left( q\zeta^2; q\right)}
    =
    \frac{\left( q\zeta^2; q\right) \left( q\zeta; q\right)}
    {\left( q\zeta; q\right) \left( q\zeta^2; q\right)} = 1,
\]
as we wanted.

\label{lem:proofs-by-pole}
Let $\alpha \in \mathbb{C}^\times$ and $d \in \mathbb{Z}$ with $d \le 0$; if $d = 0$, assume additionally that $\alpha \not\in \left\{q^n : n \in \mathbb{Z}\right\}$. Let $S$ be an open horizontal strip of length $> \textnormal{Im}\ \tau$, and suppose $F, G \in \mathcal{T}_{S \setminus I}\left(\alpha x^d\right)$ where $I \subset S$ is a set of isolated points. Then one has $F = G$ iff $F - G \in \textnormal{Hol}(S)$. Hence if $F$ and $G$ only have simple poles, it suffices to check that their residues at those poles agree.

nodes.statement: In most product identities, the nonzero 2D Fourier coefficients of entire and half-plane-entire functions tend to cluster in parabolas, such as in crefeq:triple,eq:quintuple,eq:septuple,eq:nonuple or (partly) in creftbl:plot1. But the series in crefprop:fractional have poles when x = q^n (n in Z), so their nonzero coefficients cluster in a collection of lines rather than parabolas; each line corresponds to a series of the type (1-q^nx)^-1 = sum_m ge 0 q^mnx^m or (1-q^nx)^-2 = sum_m ge 0 (m+1) q^mnx^m, indicating the order of the associated pole.

nodes.name: Proof of \cref{prop:fractional}
nodes.statement: We view the expressions in crefeq:inverse,eq:inverse2,eq:fractional as functions of z (as usual), and regard q and y as constants. Let L(z) denote the left-hand side and R(z) the right-hand side of crefeq:inverse. One can check that both sides define holomorphic functions on \0 < textnormalIm\ z < textnormalIm\ tau\, with boundaries imposed on R(z) by the convergence of sum_m ge 0 x^m (coming from n = 0), respectively sum_n ge 0 q^n x^-n (coming from m = 0); in fact, L(z) is a meromorphic in all of C. Now rewrite \[ R(z) = frac11 - x + sum_n ge 1 U_n(z) - sum_n ge 0 V_n(z) for 0 < textnormalIm\ z < textnormalIm\ tau, \] where U_n(z) = sum_m ge 0 q^(2m+1)n x^m-n and V_n(z) = sum_m ge 0 q^(2n+1)(m+1) x^m-n. This gives a meromorphic continuation of R(z) to S := \-textnormalIm\ tau < textnormalIm\ z < textnormalIm\ tau\, with poles only at x = 1 (i.e., at z = 2pi i n, n in Z). Moreover, on S cap (S - tau) = \-textnormalIm\ tau < textnormalIm\ z < 0\, this continuation satisfies \[ -x^-1 R(z + tau) &= -fracx^-11 - qx - sum_n ge 1 left(V_n(z) + x^-n-1right) + sum_n ge 0 U_n+1(z) \\ &= R(z) - frac11-x -fracx^-11 - qx + V_0(z) + fracx^-21 - x^-1 \\ &= R(z) - frac11-x -fracx^-11 - qx + fracq1-qx + fracx^-1x - 1 = R(z) + x^-1 - x^-1 \ = R(z). \] Thus R in T_S setminus Ileft(-x^-1right), where I = \x = 1\. But the same is true for L(z) = (q; q)^2 leftlangle x; qrightrangle^-1, since leftlangle x; qrightrangle in T_Cleft(-xright) only has zeros on \x = q^n : n in Z\. Furthermore, near the poles one has \[ lim_x to 1 (1 - x) L(z) = lim_x to q frac(q; q)^2 (1 - x)leftlangle x; qrightrangle = lim_x to 1 frac(q; q)^2(qx; q)left(qx^-1; qright) = 1, \] \[ lim_x to 1 (1 - x) R(z) = lim_x to 1 frac1-x1-x = 1, \] so that L - R is holomorphic on S; creflem:proofs-by-pole now completes the proof of crefeq:inverse. The proof of crefeq:fractional is analogous, by writing the right-hand side as frac11-x + sum_n ge 1 fracy^n1-q^n x - sum_n ge 1 fracq^nx^-1y^-n1-q^n x^-1 on the same punctured strip S setminus I; the relevant function space is now T_Ssetminus I(y), and the fact that y notin left\q^n : n in Zright\ (since |q| < |y| < 1) allows us to apply creflem:proofs-by-pole (again, by identifying residues at x = 1). As for crefeq:inverse2, one can proceed similarly using creflem:proofs-by-pole for the function space T_S setminus Ileft(x^-2right), except that the presence of double poles at x = 1 makes the identification harder. Alternatively, one can recover crefeq:inverse2 by taking the derivative in y of crefeq:fractional at y = q/x, and multiplying by q/x.

We view the expressions in \cref{eq:inverse,eq:inverse2,eq:fractional} as functions of $z$ (as usual), and regard $q$ and $y$ as constants. Let $L(z)$ denote the left-hand side and $R(z)$ the right-hand side of \cref{eq:inverse}. One can check that both sides define holomorphic functions on $\{0 < \textnormal{Im}\ z < \textnormal{Im}\ \tau\}$, with boundaries imposed on $R(z)$ by the convergence of $\sum_{m \ge 0} x^m$ (coming from $n = 0$), respectively $\sum_{n \ge 0} q^n x^{-n}$ (coming from $m = 0$); in fact, $L(z)$ is a meromorphic in all of $\mathbb{C}$. Now rewrite
\[
    R(z) = \frac{1}{1 - x} + \sum_{n \ge 1} U_n(z) - \sum_{n \ge 0} V_n(z)
    \qquad\qquad 
    \text{for } 0 < \textnormal{Im}\ z < \textnormal{Im}\ \tau,
\]
where $U_n(z) = \sum_{m \ge 0} q^{(2m+1)n} x^{m-n}$ and $V_n(z) = \sum_{m \ge 0} q^{(2n+1)(m+1)} x^{m-n}$. This gives a meromorphic continuation of $R(z)$ to $S := \{-\textnormal{Im}\ \tau < \textnormal{Im}\ z < \textnormal{Im}\ \tau\}$, with poles only at $x = 1$ (i.e., at $z = 2\pi i n$, $n \in \mathbb{Z}$). Moreover, on $S \cap (S - \tau) = \{-\textnormal{Im}\ \tau < \textnormal{Im}\ z < 0\}$, this continuation satisfies
\[
\begin{aligned}
    -x^{-1} R(z + \tau)
    &=
    -\frac{x^{-1}}{1 - qx} - 
    \sum_{n \ge 1} \left(V_n(z) + x^{-n-1}\right)
    +
    \sum_{n \ge 0} U_{n+1}(z)
    \\
    &= R(z) - \frac{1}{1-x} -\frac{x^{-1}}{1 - qx} + V_0(z) + \frac{x^{-2}}{1 - x^{-1}} \\
    &= R(z) - \frac{1}{1-x} -\frac{x^{-1}}{1 - qx} + \frac{q}{1-qx} + \frac{x^{-1}}{x - 1}
    \quad =
    R(z) + x^{-1} - x^{-1} \ = R(z).
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus $R \in \mathcal{T}_{S \setminus I}\left(-x^{-1}\right)$, where $I = \{x = 1\}$. But the same is true for $L(z) = (q; q)^2 \left\langle x; q\right\rangle^{-1}$, since $\left\langle x; q\right\rangle \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(-x\right)$ only has zeros on $\{x = q^n : n \in \mathbb{Z}\}$. Furthermore, near the poles one has

\[
    \lim_{x \to 1} (1 - x) L(z) = \lim_{x \to q} \frac{(q; q)^2 (1 - x)}{\left\langle x; q\right\rangle} 
    = \lim_{x \to 1} \frac{(q; q)^2}{(qx; q)\left(qx^{-1}; q\right)} = 1,
\]
\[
    \lim_{x \to 1} (1 - x) R(z) = \lim_{x \to 1} \frac{1-x}{1-x} = 1,
\]
so that $L - R$ is holomorphic on $S$; \cref{lem:proofs-by-pole} now completes the proof of \cref{eq:inverse}. The proof of $\cref{eq:fractional}$ is analogous, by writing the right-hand side as $\frac{1}{1-x} + \sum_{n \ge 1} \frac{y^n}{1-q^n x} - \sum_{n \ge 1} \frac{q^nx^{-1}y^{-n}}{1-q^n x^{-1}}$ on the same punctured strip $S \setminus I$; the relevant function space is now $\mathcal{T}_{S\setminus I}(y)$, and the fact that $y \not\in \left\{q^n : n \in \mathbb{Z}\right\}$ (since $|q| < |y| < 1$) allows us to apply \cref{lem:proofs-by-pole} (again, by identifying residues at $x = 1$).

As for \cref{eq:inverse2}, one can proceed similarly using \cref{lem:proofs-by-pole} for the function space $\mathcal{T}_{S \setminus I}\left(x^{-2}\right)$, except that the presence of double poles at $x = 1$ makes the identification harder. Alternatively, one can recover \cref{eq:inverse2} by taking the derivative in $y$ of \cref{eq:fractional} at $y = q/x$, and multiplying by $q/x$.

nodes.raw_latex:
\label{lem:m-identities}
Let $\alpha, \beta \in \mathbb{C}^\times$, and $a, b, u, v$ be positive integers. Then for $k, j \in \mathbb{Z}$ and any complete residue system $R$ of integers modulo $au^2+bv^2$, one has
\begin{equation} \label{eq:m-expansion}
    \vect{\alpha x^a}{k}(u z) \cdot \vect{\beta x^b}{j}(v z) = 
    \sum_{\ell \in R} M_\ell(q) \vect{\alpha^u \beta^v q^{a\binom{u}{2} + b \binom{v}{2}} x^{au^2+bv^2}}{\ell},
\end{equation}
where the coefficients $M_\ell(q) \in \mathbb{C}$ also depend on $a, b, \alpha, \beta, u, v$ but not on $z$, and are computed as follows. Let $d := \gcd(au, bv)$, $a' := au/d$, $b' := bv/d$ and $\ell' := (\ell - uk - vj)/d$. If $\ell' \not\in \mathbb{Z}$, then $M_\ell(q) = 0$. Else, letting $(n_0, m_0)$ be an integer solution to $a'n_0 + b'm_0 = 1$, one has
\begin{equation} \label{eq:m-coeffs-formula}
    M_\ell(q)
    =
    \gamma_\ell \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} 
    \big(\alpha^{b'} \beta^{-a'}\big)^n 
    q^{\frac{ab'^2 + ba'^2}{2}n^2 + \delta_\ell n},
\end{equation}
\[
    \gamma_\ell = \big( \alpha^{n_0} \beta^{m_0} \big)^{\ell'} q^{a\binom{n_0 \ell' }{2} + b\binom{m_0 \ell'}{2} + (kn_0 + jm_0)\ell'},
    \qquad\quad
    \delta_\ell 
    =
    (ab'n_0 - ba'm_0)\ell' - \frac{ab' - ba'}{2} + kb' - ja'.
    
\]

By \cref{lem:basic}.(iv), $S_u\left(\vect{\alpha x^a}{k}\right) \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\big(\alpha^u q^{a\binom{u}{2}} x^{au^2} \big)$ and $S_v\left(\vect{\beta x^b}{j}\right) \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\big(\beta^v q^{b\binom{v}{2}} x^{bv^2} \big)$. Hence their product lies in the product $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}$-space, which is spanned by the basis vectors on the right-hand side of \cref{eq:m-expansion} for any complete residue system $R$ modulo $au^2+bv^2$ (recall the proof of \cref{prop:polynomial-spaces}). It remains to compute the coefficients $M_\ell(q)$, i.e.\ the coefficients of $x^\ell$ in
\[
   \vect{\alpha x^a}{k}(u z) \cdot \vect{\beta x^b}{j}(v z)
   =
   \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \alpha^n q^{a\binom{n}{2} + kn} x^{aun + uk} 
    \cdot 
    \sum_{m \in \mathbb{Z}} \beta^m q^{b\binom{m}{2}+jm} x^{bvm+vj}.
\]
By multiplying these series and identifying coefficients of $x^\ell$, we find that
\[
    M_\ell(q)
    =
    \sum_{aun+bvm=\ell-uk-vj} 
    \alpha^n \beta^m q^{a\binom{n}{2} + kn + b\binom{m}{2} + jm}
    =
    \sum_{a'n + b'm = \ell'} 
    \alpha^n \beta^m q^{a\binom{n}{2} + kn + b\binom{m}{2} + jm}.
\]
Hence if $\ell' \not\in \mathbb{Z}$, there are no terms in the summation above and thus $M_\ell(q) = 0$. Otherwise, there are infinitely many terms, given precisely by
\[
    (n, m) = \ell'(n_0, m_0) + p(b', -a'), 
    \qquad\qquad p \in \mathbb{Z}.
\]
By reindexing and replacing $p$ with $n$, this yields
\[
    M_\ell(q) 
    =

\]
which simplifies to the expression in \cref{eq:m-coeffs-formula}.

Given $\alpha, \beta \in \mathbb{C}^\times$ and positive integers $a, b, u, v$, we are interested in the products below:
\begin{align}
    \label{eq:type1}
    \text{Type 1:}\qquad
    &\left\langle \alpha x^{u a}; q^a \right\rangle \left\langle \beta x^{v b}; q^b \right\rangle,
    \\
    \label{eq:type2}
    \text{Type 2:}\qquad
    &\left\langle \alpha x^{u a}; q^a \right\rangle \left\langle \alpha^2 x^{2u a}q^a; q^{2a} \right\rangle \left\langle \beta x^{v b}; q^b \right\rangle ,
    \\
    \label{eq:type3}
    \text{Type 3:}\qquad
    &\left\langle \alpha x^{u a}; q^a \right\rangle \left\langle \alpha^2 x^{2u a}q^a; q^{2a} \right\rangle \left\langle \beta x^{v b}; q^b \right\rangle \left\langle \beta^2 x^{2v b} q^b; q^{2b} \right\rangle.
\end{align}
At the same time, adequate substitutions in \cref{eq:triple,eq:quintuple} yield
\begin{align} \label{eq:substitutions-triple}
    \left(q^a; q^a\right)\left\langle \alpha x^{u a}; q^a \right\rangle 
    &= 
    \vect{-\alpha x^a}{0}(uz),
    \\
    \label{eq:substitutions-quintuple}
    \left(q^a; q^a\right) \left\langle \alpha x^{u a}; q^a \right\rangle \left\langle \alpha^2 x^{2u a}q^a; q^{2a} \right\rangle 
    &=
    \vect{\alpha^3 q^a x^{3a}}{0}(uz) 
    - 
    \alpha \vect{\alpha^3 q^a x^{3a}}{a}(uz),
\end{align}
In this context, one strategy for finding higher-order product identities proceeds as follows:
\begin{itemize}
\item[\textbf{Step}]\textbf{1.}\ Given an infinite product as in \cref{eq:type1,eq:type2,eq:type3}, use \cref{eq:substitutions-triple,eq:substitutions-quintuple} to express it as a sum of products of the form in \cref{lem:m-identities}, up to scalar factors of $\left(q^a; q^a\right)\left(q^b; q^b\right)$.

\item[\textbf{Step}]\textbf{2.}\ Apply \cref{lem:m-identities} repeatedly and group terms to obtain a representation of the given product in the canonical basis of the appropriate $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(\gamma x^d\right)$ space. Having an additional $\mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{C}}$ structure (using \cref{tbl:spaces} in case $\alpha, \beta \in \{\pm 1\}$) reduces this work by half, since in a space of the form $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(s q^c x^d\right) \cap \mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(t x^{d-2c}\right)$, the canonical basis vectors pair up (recall \cref{prop:monomial-spaces}).

\item[\textbf{Step}]\textbf{3.}\ After Step 2, the coefficients of the canonical basis vectors $\vect{\gamma x^d}{\ell}$ in the resulting expansion are linear combinations of theta-type series in $q$, as in \cref{eq:m-coeffs-formula}.
Use \cref{eq:substitutions-triple,eq:substitutions-quintuple} again, specialized at adequate values $x \mapsto f(q)$, to rewrite each of these $q$-coefficients as infinite products (when applicable). This results in product identities like \cref{eq:septuple} and \cref{eq:nonuple}.
\end{itemize}
\cref{tbl:products} gathers some results of this approach.

nodes.name: $M(2, u^2+v^2)_2$ character identity
nodes.statement: Let u, v be positive integers with gcd(u, v) = 1 and u + v odd, and set c := u^2 + v^2. Let (n_0, m_0) be an integer solution to un_0 + vm_0 = 1, and take p := v n_0 - u m_0 and r := (u-v+c)/2. Then there exist factors gamma_ell of the form (-1)^a_ell q^b_ell (depending on u, v, n_0, m_0) such that, as an identity of functions in T_Cbig(-q^binomu2 + binomv2 x^cbig) cap S_Cleft(x^u+vright), (q; q)leftlangle x^u; q rightrangle leftlangle x^v; q rightrangle = sum_ell = (u+v-c+2)/2^(u+v-1)/2 gamma_ell\ chi_pell + r^(2, c)(q) left( vect-q^binomu2 + binomv2 x^cell + vect-q^binomu2 + binomv2 x^cu+v-ell right). Moreover, each character of M(2, c)_2 (given by chi_j^(2,c)(q) for 1 le j le (c-1)/2) appears exactly once in crefeq:character-id, after applying the symmetries chi_j^(2,c)(q) = -q^j chi_j+c^(2,c)(q) = chi_c-j^(2,c)(q) as needed.

Then there exist factors gamma_ell of the form (-1)^a_ell q^b_ell (depending on u, v, n_0, m_0) such that, as an identity of functions in T_Cbig(-q^binomu2 + binomv2 x^cbig) cap S_Cleft(x^u+vright), (q; q)leftlangle x^u; q rightrangle leftlangle x^v; q rightrangle = sum_ell = (u+v-c+2)/2^(u+v-1)/2 gamma_ell\ chi_pell + r^(2, c)(q) left( vect-q^binomu2 + binomv2 x^cell + vect-q^binomu2 + binomv2 x^cu+v-ell right). Moreover, each character of M(2, c)_2 (given by chi_j^(2,c)(q) for 1 le j le (c-1)/2) appears exactly once in crefeq:character-id, after applying the symmetries chi_j^(2,c)(q) = -q^j chi_j+c^(2,c)(q) = chi_c-j^(2,c)(q) as needed.
nodes.label: cor:character-identity

nodes.statement: Take a = b = alpha = beta = 1 and R = \(u+v-c+2)/2, ldots, (u+v+c)/2\ in crefprop:general-type-1, and compute \[ p_ell \ =\ delta_ell + fracc2 \ =\ (vn_0 - um_0)ell - fracv-u2 + fracc2 \ =\ p ell + r, \] using the values d = 1 and k = j = 0 in creflem:m-identities. This produces equation crefeq:character-id, except that ell varies in R and the canonical basis vectors in the right-hand side are not paired. The pairing follows from the symmetry space S_Cleft(x^u+vright) of the left-hand side (and our adequate choice of R); the remaining value ell = (u+v+c)/2 can be ignored since by crefprop:monomial-spaces, the space T_Cbig(-q^binomu2 + binomv2 x^cbig) cap S_Cleft(x^u+vright) is spanned by the sums vect-q^binomu2 + binomv2 x^cell + vect-q^binomu2 + binomv2 x^cu+v-ell for (u+v-c+2)/2 le ell le (u+v-1)/2. Finally, it is easy to check that \[ gcd(p, c) = 1 qquadand p ell + r equiv 0 pmodc for ell equiv fracu+v+c2 pmodc, \] so that the index pell+r covers each residue classes modulo c except for 0 exactly once when R setminus \(u+v+c)/2\. Together with the aforementioned symmetries at j mapsto j+c and j mapsto c-j of the characters chi^(2,c)_j(q), this settles the second part of crefcor:character-identity.

Take $a = b = \alpha = \beta = 1$ and $R = \{(u+v-c+2)/2, \ldots, (u+v+c)/2\}$ in \cref{prop:general-type-1}, and compute
\[
    p_\ell \ =\ \delta_\ell + \frac{c}{2} 
    \ =\ (vn_0 - um_0)\ell - \frac{v-u}{2} + \frac{c}{2} 
    \ =\ p \ell + r,
\]
using the values $d = 1$ and $k = j = 0$ in \cref{lem:m-identities}. This produces equation \cref{eq:character-id}, except that $\ell$ varies in $R$ and the canonical basis vectors in the right-hand side are not paired. The pairing follows from the symmetry space $\mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(x^{u+v}\right)$ of the left-hand side (and our adequate choice of $R$); the remaining value $\ell = (u+v+c)/2$ can be ignored since by \cref{prop:monomial-spaces}, the space $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\big(-q^{\binom{u}{2} + \binom{v}{2}} x^c\big) \cap \mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(x^{u+v}\right)$ is spanned by the sums $\vect{-q^{\binom{u}{2} + \binom{v}{2}} x^{c}}{\ell} + \vect{-q^{\binom{u}{2} + \binom{v}{2}} x^{c}}{u+v-\ell}$ for $(u+v-c+2)/2 \le \ell \le (u+v-1)/2$. Finally, it is easy to check that
\[
    \gcd(p, c) = 1 \qquad\text{and}\qquad p \ell + r \equiv 0 \pmod{c}
    \qquad \text{for} \qquad 
    \ell \equiv \frac{u+v+c}{2} \pmod{c},
\]
so that the index $p\ell+r$ covers each residue classes modulo $c$ \emph{except for $0$} exactly once when $R \setminus \{(u+v+c)/2\}$. Together with the aforementioned symmetries at $j \mapsto j+c$ and $j \mapsto c-j$ of the characters $\chi^{(2,c)}_{j}(q)$, this settles the second part of \cref{cor:character-identity}.

nodes.statement: For u = 1 and v = 2 (thus c = u^2 + v^2 = 5), crefcor:character-identity recovers the septuple product identity from crefeq:septuple, which can be rephrased as \[ (q; q)leftlangle x; qrightrangle leftlangle x^2; qrightrangle = &-chi_1^(2,5)(q) left(vect-qx^51 + vect-qx^52right) \\ &+chi_2^(2,5)(q) left(vect-qx^50 + vect-qx^53right). \] For u = 2 and v = 3, one obtains the analogous result \[ (q; q)leftlangle x^2; qrightrangle leftlangle x^3; q rightrangle = &- qchi_5^(2,13)(q) left(vect-q^4 x^13-3 + vect-q^4 x^138right) \\ &- qchi_3^(2,13)(q) left(vect-q^4 x^13-2 + vect-q^4 x^137right) \\ &+ qchi_2^(2,13)(q) left(vect-q^4 x^13-1 + vect-q^4 x^136right) \\ &+ hspace0.16cm chi_6^(2,13)(q) left(vect-q^4 x^130 + vect-q^4 x^135right) \\ &+ qchi_1^(2,13)(q) left(vect-q^4 x^131 + vect-q^4 x^134right) \\ &- hspace0.16cm chi_4^(2,13)(q) left(vect-q^4 x^132 + vect-q^4 x^133right) , \] which may be linked to the Andrews--Gordon identities as explained after crefqtn:characters. On the other hand, the squared triple product identity from crefprop:squared-triple follows by taking a = b = u = v = 1 in crefprop:general-type-1 (so that au^2 + bv^2 = c = 2), a case not covered by crefcor:character-identity. Other such consequences of crefprop:general-type-1 are listed below.
nodes.raw_latex:
For $u = 1$ and $v = 2$ (thus $c = u^2 + v^2 = 5$), \cref{cor:character-identity} recovers the septuple product identity from \cref{eq:septuple}, which can be rephrased as
\[
\begin{aligned}
    (q; q)\left\langle x; q\right\rangle \left\langle x^2; q\right\rangle 
    =
    &-\chi_1^{(2,5)}(q) \left(\vect{-qx^5}{1} + \vect{-qx^5}{2}\right)
    \\
    &+\chi_2^{(2,5)}(q) \left(\vect{-qx^5}{0} + \vect{-qx^5}{3}\right).
\end{aligned}
\]
For $u = 2$ and $v = 3$, one obtains the analogous result
\[
\begin{aligned}
    (q; q)\left\langle x^2; q\right\rangle \left\langle x^3; q \right\rangle
    = &- q\chi_5^{(2,13)}(q) \left(\vect{-q^4 x^{13}}{-3} + \vect{-q^4 x^{13}}{8}\right) \\
    &- q\chi_3^{(2,13)}(q) \left(\vect{-q^4 x^{13}}{-2} + \vect{-q^4 x^{13}}{7}\right) \\
    &+ q\chi_2^{(2,13)}(q) \left(\vect{-q^4 x^{13}}{-1} + \vect{-q^4 x^{13}}{6}\right) \\
    &+ \hspace{0.16cm} \chi_6^{(2,13)}(q) \left(\vect{-q^4 x^{13}}{0} + \vect{-q^4 x^{13}}{5}\right) \\
    &+ q\chi_1^{(2,13)}(q) \left(\vect{-q^4 x^{13}}{1} + \vect{-q^4 x^{13}}{4}\right) \\
    &- \hspace{0.16cm} \chi_4^{(2,13)}(q) \left(\vect{-q^4 x^{13}}{2} + \vect{-q^4 x^{13}}{3}\right)
    ,
\end{aligned}
\]
which may be linked to the Andrews--Gordon identities \cite[Theorem 7.8]{andrews1998theory} as explained after \cref{qtn:characters}. On the other hand, the squared triple product identity from \cref{prop:squared-triple} follows by taking $a = b = u = v = 1$ in \cref{prop:general-type-1} (so that $au^2 + bv^2 = c = 2$), a case not covered by \cref{cor:character-identity}. Other such consequences of \cref{prop:general-type-1} are listed below.

nodes.name: Proof of \cref{prop:nonuple}
nodes.statement: Recall that the (first) nonuple product in crefeq:nonuple is proportional to \[ leftlangle x; q rightrangle leftlangle qx^2; q^2 rightrangle^2 leftlangle x^2; q^2 rightrangle = leftlangle x; q rightrangle leftlangle qx^2; q^2 rightrangle cdot leftlangle x^2; q rightrangle, \] which takes the type-2 form in crefeq:type2 for a = b = u = 1 and v = 2 (and alpha = beta = 1). After using crefeq:substitutions-triple,eq:substitutions-quintuple and expanding, apply creflem:m-identities twice for a = 3, b = 1, u = 1 and v = 2, leading to the exponents au^2 + bv^2 = 7 in the canonical basis vectors and ab'^2 + ba'^2 = 3 cdot 2^2 + 1 cdot 3^2 = 21 in the M_ell coefficients. Then group terms, apply crefeq:substitutions-triple with a = 21 and u = 1 for the coefficient of vectq^2x^75, and crefeq:substitutions-quintuple with a = 7 and u = 1 for the other three q-coefficients. Scaling by the appropriate q-factor now recovers crefeq:nonuple.
nodes.raw_latex:
Recall that the (first) nonuple product in \cref{eq:nonuple} is proportional to
\[
    \left\langle x; q \right\rangle \left\langle qx^2; q^2 \right\rangle^2 \left\langle x^2; q^2 \right\rangle 
    =
    \left\langle x; q \right\rangle \left\langle qx^2; q^2 \right\rangle \cdot \left\langle x^2; q \right\rangle,
\]
which takes the type-2 form in \cref{eq:type2} for $a = b = u = 1$ and $v = 2$ (and $\alpha = \beta = 1$). After using \cref{eq:substitutions-triple,eq:substitutions-quintuple} and expanding, apply \cref{lem:m-identities} twice for $a = 3, b = 1$, $u = 1$ and $v = 2$, leading to the exponents $au^2 + bv^2 = 7$ in the canonical basis vectors and $ab'^2 + ba'^2 = 3 \cdot 2^2 + 1 \cdot 3^2 = 21$ in the $M_\ell$ coefficients. Then group terms, apply \cref{eq:substitutions-triple} with $a = 21$ and $u = 1$ for the coefficient of $\vect{q^2x^7}{5}$, and \cref{eq:substitutions-quintuple} with $a = 7$ and $u = 1$ for the other three $q$-coefficients. Scaling by the appropriate $q$-factor now recovers \cref{eq:nonuple}.

\label{prop:undecuple}
In $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(q^6 x^{15} \right) \cap \mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(x^3 \right)$, one has
\[
\begin{aligned}
    \frac{(q; q)^2}{\left(q^{15}; q^{15}\right)}\left\langle x; q \right\rangle \left\langle x^2q; q^2 \right\rangle^2 &\left\langle x^2; q^2 \right\rangle \left\langle x^4q; q^2 \right\rangle
    \\
    =
    &-\left\langle -q^6; q^{15} \right\rangle \left(\vect{q^6 x^{15}}{1} + \vect{q^6 x^{15}}{2}\right) \\
    &+
    \left(\left\langle -q^7; q^{15} \right\rangle + q\left\langle -q^2; q^{15} \right\rangle\right) \left(\vect{q^6 x^{15}}{0} + \vect{q^6 x^{15}}{3}\right) \\
    &- q^2 \left\langle -1; q^{15} \right\rangle\left(\vect{q^6 x^{15}}{-1} + \vect{q^6 x^{15}}{4}\right) \\
    &- q \left\langle -q^3; q^{15} \right\rangle \left(\vect{q^6 x^{15}}{-2} + \vect{q^6 x^{15}}{5}\right) \\
    &+ q\left(\left\langle -q^4; q^{15}\right\rangle + q\left\langle -q; q^{15} \right\rangle\right) \left(\vect{q^6 x^{15}}{-3} + \vect{q^6 x^{15}}{6}\right) \\
    &- q\left\langle -q^6; q^{15} \right\rangle \left(\vect{q^6 x^{15}}{-4} + \vect{q^6 x^{15}}{7}\right) \\
    &- q^2\left\langle -q^3; q^{15} \right\rangle \left(\vect{q^6 x^{15}}{-5} + \vect{q^6 x^{15}}{8}\right) + 2q^2\left\langle -q^5; q^{15} \right\rangle\vect{q^6 x^{15}}{9}.
\end{aligned}
\]

nodes.raw_latex:
$\eta$ is a half-integral weight modular form for the full modular group $\Gamma$, and eta quotients are useful in computing bases of modular forms for congruence subgroups containing $\Gamma_0(n)$. Similarly, the generalized eta functions $\textnormal E_g$ satisfy transformation formulae at the action of $\Gamma_0(N)$ \cite[Corollary 2]{yang2004transformation}; one can design generalized eta quotients that are invariant under the action of $\Gamma_1(N)$, and use them to produce generators of function fields associated to general genus-zero congruence subgroups \cite{yang2004transformation}. The functions $\textnormal E_g$ (and a further generalization $\textnormal E_{g,h}$ thereof) were also studied in \cite{berndt1973generalized}.

For our purposes, the generalized eta functions provide the ``right'' normalization of the double infinite products $\left\langle q^g; q^N \right\rangle$, in the sense that when specializing a product identity at a value $x = \pm q^r$, all extraneous powers of $q$ will be encapsulated in the functions $\eta$ and $\textnormal E_g$; this \emph{must} be the case because (non-constant) powers of $q$ do not transform nicely under $\tau \mapsto -1/\tau$. The following lemma provides a few easy facts about $\eta$ and $\textnormal E_g$, with proofs left to the reader.

The first equality in \cref{eq:level-7-1} follows by specializing the nonuple product identity from \cref{prop:nonuple} at $x = 1$; the left-hand side of \cref{eq:nonuple} becomes null due to the factor of $\left\langle x; q\right\rangle$, and the last term in \cref{eq:nonuple} results (after suitable scaling) in the quotient $2\eta(14\tau)^2/\eta(7\tau)^2$ above.

The second equality in \cref{eq:level-7-1} is equivalent to an identity of Hickerson; indeed, by dividing the fact that $(4.6)$ equals $(4.8)$ in \cite{hickerson1988seventh} by $-q^3(q; q)\left(q^7; q^7\right)^2$ and simplifying, one obtains:
\[
\frac{\left\langle q; q^7 \right\rangle}{\left\langle q^4; q^{14} \right\rangle} - \frac{\left\langle q^2; q^7 \right\rangle}{\left\langle q^6; q^{14} \right\rangle} + \frac{\left\langle q^3; q^7 \right\rangle}{q\left\langle q^2; q^{14} \right\rangle} = \frac{\left\langle q^7; q^{14} \right\rangle}{q}.
\]
Finally, the two equalities in \cref{eq:level-7-2} follow by specializing our type-1 product identity \cref{eq:order-21} at $x = -q^{1/3}$ (and applying \cref{eq:substitutions-quintuple} with $a = 7$ for the specialization of each pair of canonical basis vectors), respectively at $x = 1$.

Identifying the coefficients of x^0, which are equal to 1 on both sides of crefeq:rogers, completes the proof of the first equality. For the second equality, it is easier to take x mapsto x^2; denote \[ L(z) := sum_n geq 0 fracq^n^2(q; q)_n x^2n qquadand R(z) := sum_n ge 0 fracq^n^2left(q^2; q^2right)_n x^2n left(-q^2n+2 x^2; q^2right), \] where R(z) is almost a twisted sum in the sense of crefeq:w-coeffs. Since L(z/2) in T_C(1, qx), one can obtain \[ L(z) - L(z+tau/2) = qx^2 L(z+tau) \\ L(z+tau/2) - L(z+tau) = q^2x^2 L(z+3tau/2) Rightarrow L in T_Cleft(1 + qx^2 + q^2 x^2, -q^5 x^4right). \\ L(z+tau) - L(z+3tau/2) = q^3x^2 L(z+2tau). \] Hence it is natural to attempt to show that R in T_Cleft(1 + qx^2 + q^2 x^2, -q^5 x^4right) as well, and this follows with little effort after expanding R(z) - left(1 + q^2 x^2right)R(z+tau). We saw in \cref{ex:two-var-rog-ram,ex:two-var-rog-ram-ctd} that $\sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n^2}}{(q; q)_n} x^n \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}(1, qx)$, and that $\dim \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}(1, qx) = \dim \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{+}\hspace{-0.03cm}}}(1, qx) = 1$. A significantly lengthier computation shows that the right-hand side lies in $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{+}\hspace{-0.03cm}}}(1, qx)$ as well; see the function $H_1$ in \cite[p.~292--294]{hardy1979introduction}. Identifying the coefficients of $x^0$, which are equal to $1$ on both sides of \cref{eq:rogers}, completes the proof of the first equality.

For the second equality, it is easier to take $x \mapsto x^2$; denote 
\[
    L(z) := \sum_{n \geq 0} \frac{q^{n^2}}{(q; q)_n} x^{2n}
    \qquad\text{and}\qquad  
    R(z) := \sum_{n \ge 0} 
    \frac{q^{n^2}}{\left(q^2; q^2\right)_n} x^{2n} \left(-q^{2n+2} x^2; q^2\right),
\]
where $R(z)$ is almost a twisted sum in the sense of \cref{eq:w-coeffs}. Since $L(z/2) \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}(1, qx)$, one can obtain
\[
    \begin{cases}
    L(z) - L(z+\tau/2) = qx^2 L(z+\tau) \\
    L(z+\tau/2) - L(z+\tau) = q^2x^2 L(z+3\tau/2) 
    \quad \Rightarrow \quad 
    L \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(1 + qx^2 + q^2 x^2, -q^5 x^4\right).
    \\
    L(z+\tau) - L(z+3\tau/2) = q^3x^2 L(z+2\tau).
    \end{cases}
\]
Hence it is natural to attempt to show that $R \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(1 + qx^2 + q^2 x^2, -q^5 x^4\right)$ as well, and this follows with little effort after expanding $R(z) - \left(1 + q^2 x^2\right)R(z+\tau)$. Now from \cref{prop:upper-bounds}.(ii) for $n_0 = -3$ one obtains that $\dim \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(1 + qx^2 + q^2 x^2, -q^5 x^4\right) \le 4$, and thus by \cref{lem:proofs-by-fourier} it suffices to check that $\widehat{L}(k) = \widehat{R}(k)$ for $k \in \{-3, -2, -1, 0\}$. But these Fourier coefficients are $0, 0, 0, 1$ respectively for both $L$ and $R$, proving that $L = R$.

The second equality in crefprop:2var-rog-ram implies crefeq:rog-ram by identifying the coefficients of x^0 as x^1, as seen in crefeq:two-variable-statement-sum. Conversely, identifying the coefficients of x^0 and x^1 is enough to prove an equality in T_H^textnormal-hspace-0.03cmleft(qx^2 - xright), by creflem:proofs-by-fourier (or in this case, directly by crefeq:fourier-coeffs-basis).

The first equality in \cref{prop:2var-rog-ram} and the membership to $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(qx^2 - x\right)$ follow immediately from the expansions
\[
    (q; q)\left\langle x; q\right\rangle = \sum_{m \in \mathbb{Z}} q^{\binom{m}{2}} (-x)^m
    \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}(-x)
    \qquad \text{and} \qquad 
    (qx; q) = \sum_{n \ge 0} (-1)^n \frac{q^{\binom{n+1}{2}}}{(q; q)_n} (-x)^n \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}(1-qx),
\]
due to \cref{eq:triple} and \cref{eq:basic1}. nodes.name: Proof that \cref{thm:twisted-rog-ram} $\Leftrightarrow$ \cref{thm:bases-proportional}
nodes.statement: Using the triple product identity in the form vect-qx0 = (q;q) left(x^-1; qright) (qx; q), one can rewrite crefthm:bases-proportional as \[ (q; q)leftlangle x^2; q rightrangle left(x^-1; qright)vectqx^2-x0 vspace0.1cm \\ left(x^-1; qright)vectqx^2-x1 = -vect-qx0 vect-qx^51 + vect-qx^52 vspace0.1cm \\ vect-qx^50 + vect-qx^53 , \] Now recall the formulae for canonical basis vectors from crefcor:kind2 (use y = 1): \[ left(x^-1; qright)vectqx^2-x0 vspace0.1cm \\ left(x^-1; qright)vectqx^2-x1 = sum_n in Z q^n^2 x^2n left(q^-n+1x^-1; qright) vspace0.1cm \\ sum_n in Z q^n^2+n x^2n+1 left(q^-nx^-1; qright) . \] As observed in the proof of crefprop:exact-formulae-kind2, the two series in the right-hand side are just twisted versions of the series vectqx^20 and vectqx^21, so they lie in T_Cleft(qx^2right). But by crefprop:monomial-spaces, we have T_Cleft(qx^2right) subset S_C(1), and so these series are invariant under x mapsto x^-1; thus \[ sum_n q^n^2 x^2n left(q^-n+1x^-1; qright) vspace0.1cm \\ sum_n q^n^2+n x^2n+1 left(q^-nx^-1; qright) = sum_n q^n^2 x^-2n (q^-n+1x; q) vspace0.1cm \\ sum_n q^n^2+n x^-2n-1 (q^-nx; q) = sum_n q^n^2 x^2n (q^n+1x; q) vspace0.1cm \\ sum_n q^n^2+n x^2n+1 (q^n+1x; q) , \] where all summations are over n in Z, and we took n mapsto -n and n mapsto -n-1 in the last equality. Overall, we have found that crefthm:bases-proportional is equivalent to (q; q) leftlangle x^2; q rightrangle sum_n in Z q^n^2 x^2n left( q^n+1x; qright) vspace0.1cm \\ sum_n in Z q^n^2 + nx^2n+1 left( q^n+1x; qright) = -vect-qx0 vect-qx^51 + vect-qx^52 vspace0.1cm \\ vect-qx^50 + vect-qx^53 . Now by applying the multiplication identities from creflem:m-identities four times, and using crefeq:substitutions-quintuple with a = 10 on each q-coefficient (as in Step 3 from crefsubsec:higher-order), we find that \[ vect-qx0 vect-qx^51 + vect-qx^52 vspace0.1cm \\ vect-qx^50 + vect-qx^53 = (q; q) A(q) & B(q) vspace0.1cm\\ C(q) & D(q) vectq^2x^62 - vectq^2x^60 vspace0.1cm \\ vectq^2x^63 - vectq^2x^6-1 , \] where A(q), B(q), C(q), D(q) are exactly as in crefeq:explicit-matrix. Hence to prove that crefthm:bases-proportional is equivalent to crefthm:twisted-rog-ram, it suffices to show that leftlangle x^2; q rightrangle vectqx^20 vspace0.1cm \\ vectqx^21 stackrel?= vectq^2x^60 - vectq^2x^62 vspace0.1cm \\ vectq^2x^6-1 - vectq^2x^63 . Now by crefeq:substitutions-triple and crefeq:substitutions-quintuple, we have \[ leftlangle x^2; q rightrangle vectqx^20 vspace0.1cm \\ vectqx^21 &= left(q^2; q^2right) leftlangle x^2; q^2 rightrangle leftlangle qx^2; q^2 rightrangle leftlangle -qx^2; q^2 rightrangle vspace0.1cm \\ xleftlangle -q^2 x^2; q^2 rightrangle \\ &= left(q^2; q^2right) leftlangle x^2; q^2 rightrangle leftlangle q^2x^4; q^4 rightrangle vspace0.1cm \\ -x^3leftlangle qx^2; q^2 rightrangle leftlangle q^4x^4; q^4 rightrangle = vectq^2x^60 - vectq^2x^62 vspace0.1cm \\ -x^3left(vectq^5x^60 - qvectq^5x^62right) , \] which simplifies to the right-hand side of crefeq:to-show-quintuple, using that qvectq^5 x^62 = vectq^5x^6-4 and x^3 in T_Cleft(q^-3right). Thus indeed crefthm:bases-proportional Leftrightarrow crefthm:twisted-rog-ram.

nodes.name: First proof of \cref{thm:twisted-rog-ram}
nodes.statement: By creflem:proofs-by-value for T_Cleft(qx^2right), it suffices to prove crefthm:twisted-rog-ram when x in \1, -1\. After noting that left(q^n+1; qright) = 0 for n < 0, the statement at x = 1 (i.e., z = 0) becomes \[ sum_n ge 0 q^n^2left(q^n+1; qright) vspace0.1cm \\ sum_n ge 0 q^n^2 + nleft(q^n+1; qright) stackrel?= A(q) & B(q) vspace0.1cm\\ C(q) & D(q) vectqx^20(0)vspace0.1cm \\ vectqx^21(0) . \] Now in last part of the previous proof, we saw (unconditionally, using creflem:m-identities) that \[ A(q) & B(q) vspace0.1cm\\ C(q) & D(q) vectqx^20vspace0.1cm \\ vectqx^21 = frac-vect-qx0(q; q)leftlangle x^2; q rightrangle vect-qx^51 + vect-qx^52 vspace0.1cm \\ vect-qx^50 + vect-qx^53 \] as an identity of meromorphic functions of z. Using that vect-qx0 = (q; q)leftlangle xq; qrightrangle and letting z to 0, our claim to prove becomes \[ sum_n ge 0 q^n^2left(q^n+1; qright) vspace0.1cm \\ sum_n ge 0 q^n^2 + nleft(q^n+1; qright) stackrel?= frac12 vect-qx^51(0) + vect-qx^52(0) vspace0.1cm \\ vect-qx^50(0) + vect-qx^53(0) \\ = sum_n in Z (-1)^n q^frac5n^2+n2 vspace0.1cm \\ sum_n in Z (-1)^n q^frac5n^2+3n2 , \] which is equivalent to the Rogers--Ramanujan identities from crefeq:rog-ram (which we deduced from crefprop:rogers), after dividing by (q; q) and applying the triple product identity.
